title: Ms. Y & The Health Service Executive
text:
Decision
Ms. Y & The Health Service Executive
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200165-A0A0M3
Published on 6 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the HSE was justified in refusing the applicant’s request for safeguarding records relating to her son on the basis that the records do not exist or cannot be found after it had taken all reasonable steps to identify and ascertain their whereabouts
6 July 2026
Background
By way of background to this case, the HSE provides long-term homecare services to the applicant’s son via a private company that acts as a service provider to the HSE. Although the applicant’s son made the original request with the support of his mother, his mother represented him from internal review stage onwards, including the application to, and interactions, with this Office. As such, all references to “ the applicant
” in this decision are references to the mother of the original requester.
On 6 May 2025, the applicant’s son made a request to the HSE for all information (electronic and otherwise), emails, reports and outcomes/results regarding safeguarding reports made by the relevant home care provider relating to him. He said that there were a number of reports starting in late 2023/early 2024 and during 2024. He also sought the same information relating to a report made by his mother on his behalf on around 18 December 2024.
On 2 October 2025, the HSE part-granted the applicant’s son’s request, releasing nine HSE records. The HSE withheld information from some of these records under section 37(1) of the FOI Act, which it said was personal information of third parties. The HSE confirmed that it had requested and obtained the applicant’s consent under section 37(2) for release of personal information relating to her but that it had neither sought nor obtained the consent of the other third parties concerned.
On 29 October, the applicant requested an internal review of the HSE’s decision, and made specific reference to what she considered to be missing records.
On 18 December, the HSE varied its original decision, releasing further records that it said it had obtained from the home care provider. The HSE labelled the home care provider records ‘File B’, while the originally released HSE safeguarding records were labelled ‘File A’. The interal reviewer affirmed the decision to refuse access to certain information in File A on the basis of section 37(1) and also withheld certain information from the File B records on the same basis.
On 16 February 2026, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of the HSE’s internal review decision. In her application, she specifically maintained that the HSE had refused to release a safeguarding plan related to a safeguarding complaint made by her in December 2024.
In the course of the review by this Office, the applicant confirmed that she was not contesting the redactions made by the HSE in the released records.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. During the course of this review, the Investigating Officer provided the applicant with details of the HSE’s submissions and offered her an opportunity to respond, which she duly did. While I do not intend to repeat either the HSE’s submissions or those of the applicant in full here, I can confirm that I have had regard to both for the purposes of this review. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
As set out above, in the course of correspondence with this Office, the applicant indicated that she was not contesting the redactions made to the relevant records on the basis of section 37(1). In the circumstances, I am satisfied that I do not need to consider this further as part of my review.
In addition, in her application to this Office, the applicant said that the HSE was refusing to release a specified safeguarding report with respect to her son. However, in the course of the review by this Office, the HSE told the Investigating Officer that the safeguarding report referred to by the applicant does not exist. This means that the HSE is effectively refusing access to the report on the basis of section 15(1)(a) of the Act which provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found.
Therefore, this Office’s review is solely concerned with whether the HSE was justified in refusing the applicant’s request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act.
Preliminary Matters
At the outset I wish to make some preliminary comments.
Firstly, this Office has no remit to investigate complaints, or to adjudicate on how FOI bodies perform their functions generally, or to act as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism with respect to actions taken by FOI bodies. Our role is confined to reviewing the decision taken by the FOI body on the applicant’s request for records.
Secondly, this Office’s review is solely concerned with the 2014 FOI Act and it is not within this Office’s remit to consider the GDPR.
Analysis and Findings
Section 15(1)(a)
Section 15(1)(a) of the Act provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. The role of this Office in a case such as this is to review the decision of the FOI body and to decide whether that decision was justified. This means that I must have regard to the evidence available to the decision maker and the reasoning used by the decision maker in arriving at their decision and also must assess the adequacy of the searches conducted by the FOI body in looking for relevant records.
The evidence in “search” cases generally consists of the steps actually taken to search for the records along with miscellaneous and other information about the record management practices of the FOI body, insofar as those practices relate to the records in question. It is also important to note that the FOI Act is concerned with access to records that a public body holds as opposed to records that a requester considers ought to exist.
As noted above, the HSE provided this Office with information on the searches that it undertook to locate relevant records, details of which were provided to the applicant. The applicant also made submissions in support of her view that further records ought to exist. While I do not propose to repeat the submissions from both parties in full here, I confirm that I have had regard to them for the purposes of this review.
The parties’ submissions
In its submissions to this Office, the HSE confirmed that the home care provider is a service provider funded by the HSE for the provision of services to the applicant’s son. According to the HSE, the home care provider has confirmed that a meeting took place with the carer in relation to the alleged incident at the time of the applicant’s complaint in December 2024 and that the carer provided a statement. The HSE also said that the home care provider deemed that the matter was not a safeguarding one and that it did not log a safeguarding report.
The HSE also confirmed that the home care provider is satisfied that it provided the HSE’s internal reviewer with all records in its possession relating to safeguarding referrals relevant to this request. The HSE said that the home care provider has confirmed that it has no safeguarding records in relation to a report made by the applicant on 18 December 2024. The HSE also said that it is satisfied that it holds no further records in relation to preliminary screening or safeguarding records from the home care provider following receipt of the applicant’s formal safeguarding complaint in December 2024. The HSE said that the Acting Principal Social Worker has confirmed that the service has not received any further records.
The HSE provided details on the searches that both it and the home care provider carried out to find relevant records. According to the HSE, both its Disability Services and its Safeguarding Service records were searched. In the Disability Services, the Service User Chart and the Service User Home Support Chart were searched, while in the Safeguarding Service, the Online System for Adult Safeguarding (OSAS) was searched. The HSE said that Disability Services are satisfied that no records exist in relation to this matter and are satisfied that records are not misfiled. The HSE said that all safeguarding records are managed under OSAS, filed under the service provider name and service user name. The HSE said that the OSAS search was completed using both the service provider and service user name.
According to the HSE, the home care provider searched its One Touch System as well as all emails and service user documentation. The HSE said that keywords used in searches included the name of the service user, the name of the applicant, the name of the service provider, the name of the Ward of Court (i.e. the applicant’s son) and the word “incident”. The HSE also listed the names of HSE staff members (Disability Services and Safeguarding Services sections), as well as staff members of the home care provider, who were consulted.
The HSE added that both it and the home care provider are satisfied that the records sought do not exist.
In her application to this Office, the applicant said that, following the alleged December 2024 incident she had unsuccessfully attempted to obtain a safeguarding report from the HSE or a follow-up with the home care provider. She referred to a number of documents, including her complaint letter to the HSE of December 2024 and a letter from a HSE Social Worker following a telephone conversation she had with the latter. The applicant also referred to a HSE telephone note of 29 April 2025 (page 29 in File A) in which the HSE Social Worker made a record of a call she had with a representative of the home care provider regarding the alleged incident. The applicant noted that, according to this record, the HSE Social Worker informed the home care provider representative that the HSE Safeguarding and Protection Team (SPT) cannot provide the information relating to the alleged incident and that the SPT only provides oversight of same.
The applicant also highlighted that the note recorded the home care provider’s representative as saying that he would seek authorisation to have the safeguarding plan given to the applicant and the Social Worker as stressing the importance of ongoing communication with the applicant as her son’s guardian, to which the home care provider’s representative agreed. In further communication with this Office, the applicant said that she had been recently told by the home care provider that it would commence an investigation into the alleged incident. She also said that the home care provider confirmed that, as per its area safeguarding log for recording all safeguarding matters in line with HSE Safeguarding Vulnerable Adults policy, no safeguarding concern or communication had been received from the HSE in relation to the incident.
As outlined above, the Investigating Officer shared details of the HSE’s submissions with the applicant, who submitted her own observations in which she continued to maintain that, despite the HSE’s submissions, the evidence points to the existence of a safeguarding report concerning the safeguarding complaint made by her on 18 December 2024. She said that the HSE phone note dated 29 April 2025 records a definite discussion about an existing safeguarding plan. The applicant attached a response from the HSE “Your Service, Your Say” (YSYS) service dated June 2026. She said that the YSYS response observes that, according to the April 2025 phone note, the HSE Safeguarding Team advised the home care provider that she was requesting a copy of the safeguarding plan and that the home care provider is recorded in the same phone note as having stated that it will seek authorisation to have the safeguarding plan given to the applicant as requested. According to the applicant, this information states that a safeguarding plan was made but she said that it was not shared or discussed with her or her son. The applicant maintained that the document clearly exists but that the home care provider has not provided same to her.
The applicant also said that, although the home care provider has told her that no safeguarding referral was made to the HSE about the incident in question, she made three reports - one to the clinical care manager, one to the Home Care Manager and copied to local Disability Services Manager, in addition to reporting to the HSE Safeguarding Team. She also said that it is quite extraordinary that the home care provider deemed that the matter was not one when she had reported it to the home care provider and had made a safeguarding complaint herself. She said that the home care provider claims that the incident did not meet the threshold for a safeguarding complaint but that the other documents prove this to be incorrect.
My Analysis
It is important to note that the FOI Act does not require absolute certainty as to the existence or location of records, as situations can arise where records are lost or simply cannot be found. What the FOI Act requires is that the public body concerned takes all reasonable steps to locate relevant records. Furthermore, it is open to this Office to find that an FOI body has satisfied the requirements of section 15(1)(a), even where records that an applicant believes ought to exist, or are known to have existed in the past, have not been located. We do not generally expect FOI bodies to carry out extensive or indefinite general searches for records simply because an applicant asserts that records sought ought to exist or did exist.
The question I must consider, therefore, is whether the HSE has taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the specific records sought.
Both the HSE and the home care provider maintain that they hold no safeguarding records relating to the complaint made by the applicant in December 2024. The applicant maintains that such records ought to exist.
I accept that the applicant reported the alleged incident both to the HSE and to the home care provider in December 2024. I also accept that the HSE Social Worker phone note of 29 April 2025 indicates that the HSE requested that the home care provider carry out a preliminary screening in relation to the alleged incident and that a subsequent safeguarding plan be put in place and shared with the applicant. However, according to the HSE’s submissions, the home care provider deemed that the matter was not a safeguarding one and therefore did not log a safeguarding report. In essence, both the HSE and the home care provider affirm that safeguarding records do not exist because they were never created. Having carefully considered the wording of the April 2025 phone note, I am satisfied that, despite the applicant’s assertion, there is no mention of an already existing safeguarding plan, only a request from the HSE that the home care provider develop one and share it with the applicant when completed.
I fully appreciate the applicant’s frustration that, despite raising her complaint in December 2024, she is not satisfied that the matter has reached a satisfactory conclusion. I also accept that the HSE phone note of April 2025 appears to give the impression that, at the very least, a preliminary screening form was to have been completed by the home care provider in respect of the alleged incident. However, the purpose of this Office’s review in cases like this is not to decide what records ought to exit or what records ought to have been created but to decide whether or not the FOI body has carried out all reasonable searches to locate records.
Having carefully considered the HSE’s submissions in this matter, I am satisfied that it has provided a sufficiently detailed and cogent explanation as to why no further records exist other than those which have been released to the applicant. Whilst I acknowledge the applicant’s arguments that further records ought to exist and I also acknowledge that the HSE appears to have requested the creation of preliminary screening records and a safeguarding plan, in the absence of any evidence to suggest that further searches are warranted in this case, I am satisfied that the HSE and the home care provider have carried out all reasonable steps to search for and provide the relevant records which are within the scope of the applicant’s request.
Accordingly, I find that the HSE was justified in refusing access to further records within the scope of the request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act on the basis that the records do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm the HSE’s decision. I find that the HSE was justified in refusing access to safeguarding records relating to the applicant’s December 2024 complaint on the basis of section 15(1)(a) of the Act.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
